questions.q: How does the EKS control plane's cost model differ from AKS's?
options: Both are completely free
Both are billed identically per node
EKS's control plane is billed hourly; AKS's standard control plane tier is free
EKS charges only for storage, never compute
questions.explain: Unlike AKS's free standard control plane tier, EKS charges an hourly fee for the managed control plane itself.

questions.q: What does the single command `eksctl create cluster` actually provision?
options: Only the EC2 worker nodes, nothing else
The VPC, the EKS control plane, and a managed node group, while also writing kubeconfig
Only an empty control plane with no networking or nodes
A Fargate profile only, never EC2-based nodes
questions.explain: eksctl create cluster is a convenience wrapper that provisions networking (VPC), the control plane, and a node group in one step, and configures kubectl access automatically.

questions.q: Why would Northbridge's fulfillment Pods, which run only a few times a day, be a good fit for a Fargate profile instead of a managed node group?
options: Fargate requires Pods to run continuously
Fargate runs each matching Pod on its own right-sized serverless compute with no EC2 instances to keep running and pay for between invocations
Managed node groups cannot run batch-style workloads at all
Fargate is only available for Windows containers
questions.explain: Fargate removes the need to keep EC2 instances provisioned and running between invocations, which suits infrequent workloads better than a steadily running managed node group.

questions.q: If an EKS cluster was created through the AWS console rather than eksctl, how do you connect kubectl to it?
options: kubectl connects automatically with no configuration
aws eks update-kubeconfig, specifying the cluster name and region
eksctl create cluster must be re-run against the existing cluster
Manually editing /etc/hosts
questions.explain: aws eks update-kubeconfig writes that cluster's connection details into the local kubeconfig, the AWS CLI equivalent of az aks get-credentials.

questions.q: Once kubectl is connected to an EKS cluster, how do Deployments, Services, and RBAC objects taught earlier in this course behave?
options: They require AWS-specific YAML fields to function
They work identically to how they work against AKS or a self-managed cluster, since EKS is standard Kubernetes underneath
Only Services work; Deployments require a separate AWS-specific resource
RBAC is disabled by default on EKS and cannot be enabled
questions.explain: EKS, like AKS, runs standard upstream Kubernetes — once connected, everyday objects and kubectl operations behave the same as on any other conformant cluster.
